question: A ticket summarizer uses the prompt "Summarize this ticket," but agents need the same three-part layout every time and results vary. Which change helps most?
optionA: State the exact format and limits
optionB: Raise the max_tokens value
optionC: Ask for a clearer, better summary here
optionD: Remove the system prompt
explanation: Claude responds best to explicit instructions, so name the output format and constraints you want. Asking for a better summary leaves Claude guessing what better means.

question: A voice assistant's replies go to a text-to-speech engine. The prompt says only "NEVER use ellipses," and other symbols that read badly still appear. Which change lets Claude generalize?
optionA: Repeat the rule in capital letters
optionB: Explain that replies are read aloud
optionC: Move the rule to the last message
optionD: Lower the max_tokens value for replies
explanation: Giving the reason behind an instruction lets Claude generalize to similar cases. Louder repetition of the same narrow rule gives it nothing to generalize from.

question: A report generator's prompt says "Do not use markdown," yet formatting keeps appearing. Which rewrite follows the prompting guidance on format control?
optionA: Say the ban is extremely important
optionB: Repeat the ban in every message
optionC: Ask for flowing prose paragraphs
optionD: Warn of a penalty for markdown
explanation: The guidance is to tell Claude what to do rather than what not to do, so describe the prose you want. Stronger versions of the same ban keep the negative framing.

question: A pipeline prompt says "Format the first section as a table." The team assumed every section would follow, but only the first does. What is the best fix?
optionA: Give Claude a longer role description
optionB: Trust Claude to infer the pattern
optionC: Add a table schema just for section one
optionD: State that it applies to every section
explanation: Recent Claude models read instructions literally and may not extend one from one item to another, so state the scope. Relying on inference is the cause of the problem.

question: A legal intake assistant keeps answering in a chatty consumer tone across every conversation. Where should the team define its job and tone?
optionA: In a role in the system prompt
optionB: In each document's metadata tags
optionC: In the tool's input schema
optionD: In the JSON output schema
explanation: A role set in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone, and even one sentence helps. Schemas shape the structure of output, not the voice of the assistant.

question: A classifier gives correct labels in evaluation, but its responses are slower than the product's latency target. What should the team try first?
optionA: Add several more few-shot examples
optionB: Try a different Claude model
optionC: Wrap the input in XML tags
optionD: Add a role to the prompt
explanation: Not every failing criterion is a prompting problem, and latency and cost can sometimes improve more easily by choosing a different model. More examples add input and do not address speed.

question: An engineer is asked to improve a prompt, but the team has no agreed definition of good and no way to measure results. What comes first?
optionA: Add examples and compare by eye
optionB: Rewrite the prompt with XML tags
optionC: Define criteria and a way to test
optionD: Move the prompt to structured output
explanation: Prompt engineering assumes clear success criteria and an empirical way to test against them. Without those, any rewrite is a guess, and comparing by eye will not show if it helped.

question: A ticket classifier has four few-shot examples, all short billing complaints. It now labels unusual tickets as billing. What is the best fix?
optionA: Add more short billing examples
optionB: Delete all of the examples from it
optionC: Move examples to a tool description
optionD: Add diverse examples with edge cases
explanation: Examples should be relevant and diverse, with edge cases, so Claude does not pick up unintended patterns. More of the same deepens the bias, and deleting them loses a reliable way to steer output.

question: Claude sometimes responds to the sample text in a prompt's few-shot examples instead of the real input that follows. What is the best structural fix?
optionA: Wrap the samples in example tags
optionB: Number the samples with plain digits
optionC: Shorten each sample to one line
optionD: Put the samples after the input
explanation: Wrapping examples in example tags, grouped in an examples tag, lets Claude distinguish them from instructions and input. Numbering or shortening leaves the boundary unclear.

question: A prompt mixes company policy, a customer's email and instructions in one block, and Claude sometimes treats a line from the email as an instruction. What should change?
optionA: Ask for the reply in XML tags
optionB: Put each content type in its own tag
optionC: Add emphasis to the policy text
optionD: Shorten the instructions to one line
explanation: Separate tags such as instructions, context and input help Claude parse a mixed prompt and reduce misinterpretation. Tags on the output do nothing to separate the parts of the input.

question: An assistant answers a question about a 60-page contract pasted into the prompt. The team is deciding the order of the parts. Which order follows the long-context guidance?
optionA: Question first, then the contract
optionB: Examples first, contract in the middle
optionC: Contract first, then the question
optionD: Question inside the contract text
explanation: Long documents go near the top, above the query, instructions and examples, because a query at the end can improve quality. Leading with the question is the common habit the guidance corrects.

question: A compliance workflow must log each intermediate draft, have a person inspect it, and branch on what they find before revision continues. Which design fits?
optionA: One prompt with numbered steps
optionB: One request with higher effort
optionC: One call that returns all drafts
optionD: Separate API calls for each step
explanation: Explicit chaining is still useful when you must inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a pipeline, since each call can be logged, evaluated or branched. A single call gives no point to stop and inspect.

question: Generated marketing copy often misses brand rules. The team wants the most common chaining pattern for self-correction. Which sequence is it?
optionA: Draft, review against criteria, refine
optionB: Review the rules, draft, then publish
optionC: Draft, translate, then shorten
optionD: Draft three times, keep the longest
explanation: Self-correction generates a draft, has Claude review it against criteria, then refines it from that review. The review needs a draft to act on, so it cannot come first.

question: A team is writing the success criterion for a sentiment classifier. Which criterion is the strongest?
optionA: It classifies sentiment well
optionB: F1 of 0.85 on a held-out set
optionC: Reviewers feel the labels look right
optionD: As accurate as it can possibly be
explanation: Good criteria are specific and measurable, like a named metric and target on a defined set. The other choices cannot be checked objectively or give no point at which to stop.

question: An assistant analyzing financial reports invents figures when a report lacks the needed data. What is the simplest first fix?
optionA: Ask for a more detailed analysis
optionB: Require a figure in every answer
optionC: Let Claude say it lacks the data
optionD: Raise the max_tokens value
explanation: Explicitly giving Claude permission to admit uncertainty can drastically reduce false information. Requiring a figure in every answer pushes it toward inventing one.

question: A tool reviews a very long privacy policy and sometimes cites clauses that are not in it. Which prompt change best grounds its answers?
optionA: Summarize the policy, then analyze
optionB: Ask for a confidence score on each
optionC: Ask for a shorter final analysis
optionD: Extract exact quotes, then analyze
explanation: For long documents, have Claude extract word-for-word quotes first and base the analysis on them. A summary is a rewording, so it does not tie the claims to the actual text.

question: A firm has added quote extraction, citations and permission to say "I don't know" to a tool that informs high-stakes client advice. Can it skip human validation?
optionA: No, keep validating critical facts
optionB: Yes, quotes rule out fabrication
optionC: Yes, once output is valid JSON
optionD: Yes, after one more prompt pass
explanation: These techniques significantly reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them, so critical information still needs validating. Valid JSON only shows the shape is right, not that the content is.

question: A review pipeline has a separate verification stage that ranks and filters findings. What should the first stage's prompt ask Claude to do?
optionA: Report only high-severity findings
optionB: Report all, with confidence and severity
optionC: Report only findings it is sure of
optionD: Report just the three most serious bugs found
explanation: When a later stage filters, the finding stage's job is coverage, with confidence and severity attached for ranking. Filtering early silently drops real bugs that the later stage never sees.

question: After adding "be conservative" and "don't nitpick" to a code review prompt, fewer bugs are reported though Claude investigates just as deeply. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: Claude's bug-finding skill got worse
optionB: The diff overflowed the context
optionC: Claude is following the stated bar
optionD: The prompt lacks XML tags
explanation: Claude can find an issue and then not report it because it falls below the bar the prompt sets, so precision rises and measured recall falls. Investigation depth is unchanged, which points to the prompt rather than ability.

question: A code review bot must self-filter in one pass, and "only report important bugs" gives inconsistent results. What is the best prompt change?
optionA: Ask for more caution on each finding
optionB: Repeat that only important bugs count
optionC: Add a senior reviewer role
optionD: Define concretely what gets reported
explanation: A concrete threshold, such as bugs that cause incorrect behavior but not style preferences, works better than qualitative words like important. Repeating the word leaves it just as undefined.

question: An invoice extractor must return JSON matching a schema, but its parser breaks on stray text around the JSON. What is the most direct fix?
optionA: Use JSON outputs with a schema
optionB: Ask for JSON in stronger language
optionC: Clean the reply with a regex
optionD: Add a JSON example to the prompt
explanation: JSON outputs through output_config.format use constrained decoding so the text response matches your schema. Prompting and regex cleanup can help but give no such guarantee.

question: A team moves an older prompt, which prefilled an opening brace to force JSON, to a newer Claude model. The request now returns a 400 error. What should they do?
optionA: Prefill a longer JSON fragment
optionB: Move to structured outputs
optionC: Retry until the error clears
optionD: Send the prefill as a tool result
explanation: Prefilling the last assistant turn is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models, and structured outputs are the designed replacement. A longer prefill fails the same way.

question: A router must return exactly one of six department labels and parsing free text keeps failing. Which approach does the guidance suggest for classification?
optionA: Free text mapped by keywords
optionB: A string with a long description
optionC: An enum of labels in the schema
optionD: A list of labels after the input
explanation: For classification, use a tool with an enum field holding the valid labels, or structured outputs. A plain string, however well described, is not limited to those labels.

question: A booking agent's tool needs an integer for passengers, but non-strict calls sometimes send "two" and the function fails. What is the best fix?
optionA: Lengthen the tool's description
optionB: Add a retry after each failure
optionC: Set tool_choice to none
optionD: Set strict: true on the tool
explanation: Strict tool use constrains sampling so tool inputs match the schema, with correctly typed arguments. A better description helps tool selection but does not guarantee types, and a retry only reacts to the failure.

question: An extractor sets tool_choice to any, but its Claude model rejects forced tool use with a 400 error. It still needs schema-valid tool inputs. What should the team do?
optionA: Use auto with a strict tool
optionB: Set tool_choice to none
optionC: Prefill the tool call block
optionD: Name the tool in tool_choice
explanation: Where forced tool use is rejected, the documented path is auto with strict tool use, or structured outputs for a fixed JSON reply. Naming one tool is also forced use, so it fails the same way.

question: A receipt extractor has a required string field for tax ID, and Claude invents one when none is printed. Downstream code expects every key to be present. Which schema change fits?
optionA: Make it optional, drop the key
optionB: Allow null, keep it required
optionC: Make it an enum of known IDs
optionD: Add a pattern for tax ID formats
explanation: A required field that allows null keeps every key present, and with a prompt line saying to use null when no ID is printed, Claude has an honest value for missing data. Dropping the key breaks the downstream code, and an enum or a pattern still forces Claude to produce an ID.

question: A support router's enum has five categories, and tickets that fit none get forced into a wrong one. Reports still need a fixed set of labels. What is the best schema fix?
optionA: Replace the enum with free text
optionB: Limit the field's length
optionC: Add an "other" value to the enum
optionD: Make the field an array of labels
explanation: An enum constrains output to its values, so it needs an honest choice for what fits nothing. Free text would lose the fixed set that reports depend on, and schema compliance alone never makes a forced label correct.

question: A router using an enum label sees a value that differs from the schema only in capitalization. The response completed normally with no error. How should the code handle this?
optionA: Treat it as a refusal and stop
optionB: Add a separate regex for each of the labels
optionC: Raise max_tokens and resend
optionD: Compare labels case-insensitively
explanation: Structured outputs do not guarantee the capitalization of string enum and const values, so compare case-insensitively and avoid values differing only in case. A normal stop reason shows this is not a refusal.

question: A raw API request for JSON output uses minimum and maximum on a 1-to-5 rating field and returns a 400 error. Which schema change keeps the range enforced?
optionA: Use an integer enum of 1 to 5
optionB: Describe the range in the field
optionC: Add a pattern for the integer
optionD: Set additionalProperties to true
explanation: Numerical constraints are not supported in these schemas, while scalar enums are, so listing the values enforces the range. A description is only guidance, and additionalProperties must be false on objects.

question: A JSON schema includes a step_by_step_reasoning property, and some responses come back with stop_reason refusal and category reasoning_extraction. What is the best change?
optionA: Rename it to thinking_steps
optionB: Ask for a short explanation
optionC: Mark the property as optional
optionD: Raise the max_tokens value
explanation: A property asking for the model's step-by-step reasoning can trigger this refusal, so ask for a short explanation instead. A new name that asks for the same thing does not change the request.

question: A strict-schema extractor gets a response with stop_reason max_tokens, and its text fails to parse. What is the documented way to handle it?
optionA: Close the braces and parse it
optionB: Loosen the schema and resend
optionC: Retry with a higher max_tokens
optionD: Treat it as a safety refusal
explanation: A response cut off at max_tokens may be incomplete and not match the schema, so retry with a higher limit. Repairing the JSON by hand would accept a record with missing data.

question: An invoice extraction passes the schema, but code finds line items that do not sum to the stated total. What is the best retry design?
optionA: Resend the same request unchanged
optionB: Tighten the schema's field types
optionC: Accept it, since the schema passed
optionD: Resend with the failed check named
explanation: Schema compliance does not mean values are accurate, so run business checks and give Claude the specific failure to correct. Identical resends give no new information, and types cannot express a sum. If the document itself is wrong, route it to a person.

question: A service assumes any 200 response from a structured output request holds schema-valid JSON, and its parser crashes on some replies. What should it do first?
optionA: Check stop_reason before parsing
optionB: Retry all replies with a 200
optionC: Silently skip parser errors
optionD: Add more required properties
explanation: A refusal arrives as a 200 with stop_reason refusal, and its output might not match the schema, so branch on stop_reason first. Silently skipping errors would hide those records.

question: An overnight job sends 20,000 product reviews in one Message Batch, then writes results to a database by their position in the input. Records end up mismatched. What is the best fix?
optionA: Sort results by creation time
optionB: Match results by custom_id
optionC: Send one review per batch
optionD: Stream results as they finish
explanation: Result order is not guaranteed, so give each request a meaningful custom_id and match on it. Streaming is not supported in batch requests.

question: A checkout fraud check must answer the shopper within seconds. An engineer proposes the Message Batches API to reduce cost. What is the best decision?
optionA: Use batches and poll every second
optionB: Use batches with streaming on
optionC: Use standard Messages API calls
optionD: Use one nightly batch of checkouts
explanation: Batches suit work that does not need an immediate response, and each may take up to 24 hours. Polling faster cannot speed up asynchronous processing, and batch requests do not accept streaming.

question: A finished Message Batch has mostly succeeded results, with some errored and some expired. What is the best next step?
optionA: Resubmit the entire batch as is
optionB: Discard the batch as a failure
optionC: Wait for the expired items to finish on their own
optionD: Fix errors, resubmit only the failures
explanation: Requests are processed independently, so one failure does not affect the others, and only the unsuccessful ones need another run. Invalid requests must be fixed first, and an expired request was never sent and will not finish later.

question: A team has a known correct label for each of 5,000 tickets and wants to grade a classifier prompt. Which grading method fits best?
optionA: Exact match to the known label
optionB: Human reading of every reply
optionC: ROUGE-L against the label text
optionD: Cosine similarity to a summary
explanation: Exact match, after normalizing case and whitespace, suits categorical tasks and can be automated. ROUGE-L measures summary overlap, and hand reading gives up automated volume.

question: A team can build either 50 carefully hand-graded evaluation cases or 2,000 automatically graded ones with somewhat lower signal per case. Which does the guidance favor?
optionA: The 50 hand-graded cases
optionB: The 2,000 automated cases
optionC: Neither until grading is perfect
optionD: Only the 10 hardest cases
explanation: The guidance prioritizes volume, preferring many automatically graded questions over a few high-quality hand-graded ones. Waiting for perfect grading delays any measurement at all.

question: A team wants to measure the empathy of Claude's support replies on a 1-to-5 scale with an LLM grader. Which design follows the guidance?
optionA: Self-rating by the same model
optionB: Exact match to a reference reply
optionC: Likert rating by a different model
optionD: ROUGE-L against a reference reply
explanation: An LLM-based Likert scale fits subjective qualities, and the grader should be a different model from the one that wrote the output. Exact match and ROUGE-L measure text overlap, not empathy.

question: A prompt scores well on an evaluation set of clean, typical tickets, but production fails on sarcasm, typos and irrelevant messages. What should the team change?
optionA: Raise the bar on the clean tickets
optionB: Run the clean tickets more often
optionC: Exclude the failing kinds of ticket
optionD: Add those edge cases to the set
explanation: Evaluations should mirror the real task distribution and include edge cases such as irrelevant input and ambiguity. More runs on clean data keep measuring the part that already works.
